youtube_title: He Misused a Police Database for Cash — Not 'Hacking,' Said the Court 🦝⚖️
caption: Van Buren v. United States (2021): an officer who sold a license-plate lookup didn't 'exceed authorized access' under the CFAA because he was allowed to access that data. Other laws and consequences still apply.
script: A cop took cash to search a police database, and the Supreme Court said it wasn't hacking. [disclaimer] This is Van Buren versus United States, from twenty twenty one. A police sergeant in Georgia took money to look up a license plate in a police database. Plot twist! The whole thing was an FBI sting. He used his own real login. But looking it up for cash broke his department's rules. So he got convicted under a big federal hacking law, for going beyond his allowed access. But the Supreme Court flipped it! The question was simple. What does going beyond your allowed access actually mean? The majority said it means getting into parts of a computer system that are off limits to you. Think of a locked door you're not supposed to open. It does not mean using a part you're allowed into, for a bad reason. He was allowed to look up license plates. So this hacking law didn't fit! Not everyone agreed. Three justices said using a police database like that should count as a crime. Here's the limit. Selling police information did not become legal. Other criminal laws, getting fired, and privacy rules are a whole separate thing. And sneaking into parts of a system you aren't allowed into is still covered by the hacking law. [loop] So before you call every misuse of a login hacking, remember
